title: Newtonian stress and Fourier conductive closure

items.title: Newtonian stress and Fourier conductive closure
items.design_state: Step 1 draft authored; readiness recorded separately.
items.physical_scope: An adopted smooth, single-component Newtonian/Fourier closure with an isotropic symmetric linear viscous response, specified nonnegative shear and bulk coefficient laws, and a tensor-valued conductivity whose symmetric part is positive semidefinite; anisotropic conduction is allowed. No coefficient is inferred from a measurement and no universal fluid applicability is asserted.
items.statement:
Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. These specified constitutive functions are adopted model inputs, not measured coefficient values or consequences of balance laws.

items.title: Constant-density incompressible Newtonian model
items.design_state: Step 1 draft authored; readiness recorded separately.
items.physical_scope: A smooth, unforced, constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch in a Cartesian inertial chart, with a pressure multiplier and constant nonnegative shear viscosity. Boundary and initial data are separate, and no solution existence or empirical applicability is asserted.
items.statement:
Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval. Use the Cartesian inertial-chart convention of the adopted continuum balances on Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$: $E$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space, and the event-coordinate map is $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$ with $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry and $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant. Time is absolute and measured in seconds, spatial coordinates in metres, and $w$ in metres per second. All derivatives below use this fixed chart. Let $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ be open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$ measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$ measured in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

items.title: Local simple-fluid equilibrium and Gibbs closure
items.design_state: Step 1 draft authored; readiness recorded separately.
items.physical_scope: An adopted local-equilibrium state relation for a smooth single-component simple-fluid branch with positive density and temperature. No global equilibrium, global thermodynamic chart, universal material validity or empirical measurement is asserted.
items.statement:
Use a smooth single-component, nonpolar fluid branch in a Cartesian inertial frame. Let $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be an open state domain with coordinates $v$ and $s$, where $v$ is specific volume and $s$ is specific entropy. Adopt a specific internal-energy function $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$, meaning that its coordinate partial derivatives through total order two exist and are continuous. At a state $(v,s)$, define the temperature and thermodynamic pressure by
$$ T(v,s)=\frac{\partial e}{\partial s}(v,s),\qquad p(v,s)=-\frac{\partial e}{\partial v}(v,s),\qquad \rho=\frac1v, $$
where each partial derivative holds the other state coordinate fixed. Assume the local material states lie in $\mathcal U$ and $T>0$. Local equilibrium here means that the fields $e,T,p$ at each event are assigned by these state functions of the local $v,s$.

In the physical SI interpretation, $v$ is in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $e$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $T$ in $\mathrm K$, $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Positivity of $e_{ss}$, global invertibility of $s\mapsto T$, convexity, and the dynamical entropy inequality are separate assumptions or postulates; none follows from this local equilibrium adoption. This closure is an additional physical model choice, not a consequence of global equilibrium thermodynamics.

items.title: Positive-response linear sound in adopted barotropic fluid
items.design_state: Step 1 draft authored; readiness recorded separately.
items.physical_scope: First variation about a uniform rest state of the adopted smooth, positive-density barotropic model when its pressure law is the fixed-entropy restriction of the adopted local state relation. The prediction is linear; no finite-amplitude error, lifespan, material measurement or empirical sound-speed claim is asserted.
items.statement:
Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ a nonempty open domain for the model fields. Let $e\in C^2(\mathcal U)$ be the local specific-energy relation on an open $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, with state coordinates $(v,s)$, $T=e_s$, and $p=-e_v$; each state partial derivative holds the other coordinate fixed. Fix $(v_b,s_b)\in\mathcal U$ with $T_b>0$ and $e_{ss}(v_b,s_b)>0$, set $\rho_b=1/v_b$, and take a barotropic pressure law $P\in C^1((0,\infty))$ that agrees with $p(1/\rho,s_b)$ on an open density interval $J_\rho\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $\rho_b$, with $(1/\rho,s_b)\in\mathcal U$ for every $\rho\in J_\rho$. This is the fixed-entropy restriction of the adopted local state relation. The smooth barotropic Euler model is linearized about the uniform rest state $(\rho,u)=(\rho_b,0)$. For $C^2$ perturbation fields $\delta\rho:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and $w:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, the first variation at $\varepsilon=0$ after $\rho=\rho_b+\varepsilon\delta\rho$, $u=\varepsilon w$ is
$$ \partial_t\delta\rho+\rho_b\operatorname{div}w=0,\qquad \rho_b\partial_tw+P'(\rho_b)\nabla\delta\rho=0,\qquad \partial_{tt}\delta\rho=c_s^2\Delta\delta\rho, \quad c_s^2=P'(\rho_b)=v_b^2e_{vv}(v_b,s_b). $$
The sign of $c_s^2$ is not assumed in the base model. If $c_s^2>0$, define $c_s=\sqrt{c_s^2}$. For every nonzero $k\in\mathbb R^3$, with $\omega=c_s|k|$, the fields
$$ \delta\rho=A\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t),\qquad w=\frac{\omega A}{\rho_b|k|^2}k\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t) $$
solve the first-variation system for every real amplitude $A$. They are exact solutions of the linearized equations, not finite-amplitude approximations with an automatic error or lifespan bound. No empirical value of $c_s$ is asserted.

In SI units, $t$ is in seconds, $x$ in metres, $\rho_b,\delta\rho,A$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u,w,c_s$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $k$ in $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $\omega$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $c_s^2$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$.

items.title: Perfect-gas entropy, isentropic law and temperature balance
items.design_state: Step 1 draft authored; readiness recorded separately.
items.physical_scope: Conditional smooth local-equilibrium calculation for an explicitly adopted calorically perfect gas with positive specific gas constant and specific heat. The temperature equation includes stress, heat flux and heat supply; entropy constancy and the isentropic pressure law are restricted to the stated adiabatic, inviscid, unsourced branch. No empirical gas data or universal gas model is asserted.
items.statement:
Assume the complete smooth material, state, contact and mass/momentum/angular-momentum/total-energy balance hypotheses of the mathematical Gibbs-entropy identity, including $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as stated in Facts & Assumptions. Let $R>0$ be a specific gas constant and $c_v>0$ a constant specific heat at constant volume, both in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. Choose reference values $T_{\mathrm{ref}}>0$ in $\mathrm K$, $\rho_{\mathrm{ref}}>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, and $s_{\mathrm{ref}}$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. On $v>0,\ s\in\mathbb R$, adopt
$$ T(v,s)=T_{\mathrm{ref}}\exp\!\left(\frac{s-s_{\mathrm{ref}}}{c_v}\right) \left(\frac{1}{\rho_{\mathrm{ref}}v}\right)^{R/c_v},\qquad e(v,s)=c_vT(v,s),\qquad p(v,s)=\frac{R\,T(v,s)}{v}. $$
These formulas give $T=e_s>0$, $p=-e_v$, and $e\in C^2((0,\infty)\times\mathbb R)$; equivalently, with $\rho=1/v$, $s=s_{\mathrm{ref}}+c_v\ln(T/T_{\mathrm{ref}})-R\ln(\rho/\rho_{\mathrm{ref}})$ and $p=\rho RT$. The logarithms have dimensionless arguments.

For a smooth solution, define $\theta=\operatorname{div}u$, $\sigma=-pI_3+\tau$, and the local entropy residual $\mathcal G=\rho D_ts+\operatorname{div}(q/T)-\rho r/T$. The temperature balance is
$$ \rho c_vD_tT=-p\theta+\tau:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r. $$
On the additional adiabatic, inviscid, unsourced branch $\tau=0,\ q=0,\ r=0$, one has $D_ts=0$. Along any trajectory on which the entropy value is $s_0$, the pressure law is
$$ p=K(s_0)\rho^\gamma,\qquad \gamma=1+\frac{R}{c_v},\qquad K(s_0)=RT_{\mathrm{ref}}\exp\!\left(\frac{s_0-s_{\mathrm{ref}}}{c_v}\right) \rho_{\mathrm{ref}}^{-R/c_v}>0. $$
Here $\gamma$ is dimensionless and $K(s_0)$ has SI units $\mathrm{Pa}\,(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}})^{-\gamma}$, so $K(s_0)\rho^\gamma$ has units of pressure. The factor $K(s_0)$ can differ between trajectories with different entropy values. The gas closure is an adopted model, and the adiabatic conclusion does not apply when viscous work, heat conduction, or heat supply is present.

items.title: Closed smooth incompressible kinetic-energy dissipation
items.design_state: Step 1 draft authored; readiness recorded separately.
items.physical_scope: Conditional kinetic-energy identity for an actual smooth unforced, constant-density incompressible Newtonian solution on a fixed no-slip domain or periodic domain. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, long-time regularity, global solution or empirical realization.
items.statement:
Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval containing $0$. Use SI units: time is measured in seconds, spatial coordinates and lengths in metres, $\rho_0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $\mu$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. A bounded $C^1$ domain means a bounded open set locally on one side of a continuously differentiable boundary graph. The fixed spatial region $\Omega$ is either a nonempty bounded $C^1$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ or one rectangular period cell $[0,L_1]\times[0,L_2]\times[0,L_3]$ with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres. In the bounded-domain case, let $\mathcal O\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ be open and contain $I\times\overline\Omega$, and suppose $u\in C^2(\mathcal O,\mathbb R^3)$ and $p\in C^1(\mathcal O,\mathbb R)$. In the periodic case, take $u$ and $p$ on $I\times\mathbb R^3$, periodic with their derivatives on opposite faces of the stated cell. In either case suppose the smooth fields satisfy on the stated spacetime domain the pointwise constant-density incompressible Newtonian model equations
$$ \rho=\rho_0>0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $\mu\ge0$ is constant, the body force is zero, $D=(\nabla u+\nabla u^T)/2$, $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, and $\operatorname{div}\sigma$ is the rowwise divergence. In the bounded-domain case impose the no-slip condition $u=0$ on $I\times\partial\Omega$; in the periodic case the model equations hold on the periodic lift to $\mathbb R^3$.

For matrices $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ define the Frobenius contraction $A:B:=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$ and the squared norm $|D|^2:=D:D=\sum_{i,j=1}^3D_{ij}^2$. Let $E_k(t)=\frac{\rho_0}{2}\int_\Omega |u(t,x)|^2\,dx$, using one period cell in the periodic case. For every $t_1<t_2$ in $I$,
$$ E_k(t_2)+2\mu\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\int_\Omega |D(t,x)|^2\,dx\,dt=E_k(t_1). $$
Thus $E_k$ is nonincreasing; strict decay is not claimed when $D$ vanishes. The theorem is conditional on an actual smooth solution and supplies no existence or long-time regularity result.

items.title: Negative bulk viscosity violates entropy admissibility
items.design_state: Step 1 draft authored; readiness recorded separately.
items.physical_scope: Algebraic counterexample in the Newtonian/Fourier residual family with negative bulk coefficient. This coefficient lies outside the adopted nonnegative-bulk postulate; the example is not a material observation or claim about a realized fluid.
items.statement:
Let $\operatorname{Sym}(3)=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and let $I_3$ be the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ set $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, and $|D_0|^2=\sum_{i,j=1}^3(D_0)_{ij}^2$. For $\mu\ge0$, $\zeta\in\mathbb R$, $K\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $g\in\mathbb R^3$, and $T>0$, define the pointwise Newtonian/Fourier residual
$$\mathcal G(D,g,T)=\frac{2\mu|D_0|^2+\zeta\theta^2}{T}+\frac{g^T\operatorname{sym}(K)g}{T^2},\qquad \operatorname{sym}(K)=\frac{K+K^T}{2}.$$
Here $g$ is the temperature-gradient value; in SI units $D$ is in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $g$ in $\mathrm{K\,m^{-1}}$, and $\mathcal G$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$. The false assertion is that $\mathcal G(D,g,T)\ge0$ for every such $D,g,T$ whenever $\mu\ge0$, independently of the value of $\zeta$.

references.title: David Tong, Fluid Mechanics, Part II lecture notes
An Introduction to Continuum Mechanics, Second Edition, Chapter 6

items.title: Negative acoustic response yields exponential mode growth
items.design_state: Step 1 draft authored; readiness recorded separately.
items.physical_scope: Exact counterexample for the linearized equations of an explicitly adopted smooth barotropic state relation with negative fixed-entropy pressure response. It is not a finite-amplitude solution or an empirical claim about a realized material.
items.statement:
Let $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be open and let $e\in C^2(\mathcal U)$, with $T=e_s$ and $p=-e_v$ (each partial derivative holds the other state coordinate fixed). Fix $(v_b,s_b)\in\mathcal U$ with $T_b=e_s(v_b,s_b)>0$ and $e_{ss}(v_b,s_b)>0$, and put $\rho_b=1/v_b$. Let $P\in C^1((0,\infty))$ agree with $-e_v(1/\rho,s_b)$ on an open interval $J_\rho\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $\rho_b$, with $(1/\rho,s_b)\in\mathcal U$ for every $\rho\in J_\rho$, and suppose $P'(\rho_b)<0$. For any nonempty open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, let $\delta\rho\in C^2(I\times\mathbb R^3,\mathbb R)$ and $w\in C^2(I\times\mathbb R^3,\mathbb R^3)$ solve the first-variation equations about the uniform rest state $(\rho,u)=(\rho_b,0)$,
$$\partial_t\delta\rho+\rho_b\operatorname{div}w=0,\qquad \rho_b\partial_tw+P'(\rho_b)\nabla\delta\rho=0,$$
where $\operatorname{div}w=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}w_i$ and $\nabla\delta\rho=(\partial_{x_i}\delta\rho)_{i=1}^3$. The false assertion is that for every such state and solution, at each fixed $x\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\sup_{t\in I}\left(|\delta\rho(t,x)|+\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^3w_i(t,x)^2}\right)<\infty.$$
In SI units, $t$ is in seconds, $x$ in metres, $v_b$ in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $s_b$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $e$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $T_b$ in kelvins, $p$ and $P$ in pascals, $\rho_b$ and $\delta\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, and $w$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
